newsitem.title: USA: G7 may daze but not knock out dlr rally - US traders.
newsitem.headline: G7 may daze but not knock out dlr rally - US traders.

text.p: New York foreign exchange traders said the Group of Seven's (G7) statement over closer currency alignment might erode the value of the dollar in the near-term, but they expressed confidence the greenback would rise to new highs in the longer term.

"The ball is back in the United States' court. Look for people starting to accumulate long-dollar positions after things settle," said John Gariano, a vice president and corporates trader at Sumitomo Bank New York on Sunday.

"I don't see anything that indicates a change in policy," he said, regarding an official statement issued Saturday after a much-anticipated meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bank governors in Berlin.
Dealers and economists said the statement's most significant point was that the major currency misalignments noted in its April 1995 communique "have been corrected".

The rest of the statment -- that exchange rates should reflect economic fundamentals, excess volatility is undesirable and that the group had agreed to monitor developments and cooperate as appropriate -- was "a mismash" from previous G7 communiques and provided little insight, said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT.
"I would have expected something stronger out of the G7. This statement leaves the scope for the dollar to appreciate in some manner," Rothfield said.
But don't expect a roaring dollar at the start of Asian trade on Monday, cautioned Steven Walker, a senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken New York.
"I don't think they have given everyone a green light to continue buying dollars," Walker said. "I wouldn't be surprised if we see a little bit more of a correction."
Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long Term Credit Bank of Japan in New York, agreed.

"My sense is, short-term, it was maybe slightly dollar bearish," Pettit said. "But the fact that they are still saying that currencies are governed by their economic fundamentals does leave room for flexibility on the upside," he added.

Traders interviewed said the expected outperformance of the U.S. economy to that of Japan and most of continental Europe would be the engine behind a stronger dollar this year, even despite a threat of official resistance overseas.

"The smart money is saying we have to go where we see the strong economic growth and somewhat stable financial markets and the only place you are seeing that is the United States," Sumitomo's Gariano said.
"That is going to continue to add pressure to the dollar on the upside," he said, adding he would not expect Federal Reserve intervention until the dollar hits at least 1.76 marks and 135 yen.

At the G7 summit, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the subject of intervention was not even discussed while British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said the G7 did not reach any agreement on concerted intervention.
The dollar hit a fresh four-year high at 124.72 yen and a 32-month peak at 1.6755 marks on Friday before comments from U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin sparked a furious selloff.

Rubin's cryptic message -- "We have had a strong dollar for some time now" -- was quickly interpreted here as a statement that the United States had joined the chorus from Germany and Japan which favored capping the dollar's rise at current levels.
"If anything, I think Rubin's remarks on Friday were stronger than the G7 statement," said NationsBanc's Rothfield.
